sections.normalized_html:
Let [MATH: s] be the length of the shortest side. Then, we have the following diagram.

Here, in rectangle [MATH: ABCD,]

  • the length of the diagonal [MATH: \overline{AC}] is [MATH: 2] times the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC},] and

  • the length of the longest side [MATH: \overline{AB}] is [MATH: \sqrt{3}] times the length of the shortest side [MATH: \overline{BC}.]

Thus, we have: [MATH: {AC}:{AB} = 2:\sqrt{3}]

Now, since in the right triangle [MATH: ABC,] the ratio of the hypotenuse to the longest leg is [MATH: \dfrac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{longest}} = \dfrac{AC}{AB} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}},] we have that [MATH: \triangle ABC] is a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle.

Recall that the area of a [MATH: 30^\circ]-[MATH: 60^\circ]-[MATH: 90^\circ] triangle whose shortest side has length [MATH: s] is given by [MATH: A = \dfrac{\sqrt 3}{2} s^2.]

The area of [MATH: \triangle ADC] is half the area of the rectangle: [MATH: A = \dfrac{1}{2} \cdot 108\sqrt{3} = 54\sqrt{3}]

Thus, we have the following equation that can be solved for [MATH: s{:}] [MATH: (sqrt(3))/(2)s^{2}|= 54sqrt(3); sqrt(3)s^{2}|= 108sqrt(3); s^{2}|= 108; s|= sqrt(108); = sqrt(36 ⋅ 3); = 6sqrt(3)]

Therefore, the shortest side of the rectangle is [MATH: BC = s= 6\sqrt{3} \: \text{in}.]
